newsitem.title: GERMANY: German government under pressure over joblessness.
newsitem.headline: German government under pressure over joblessness.

text.p: Blame for Germany's stubbornly high unemployment levels resides largely with Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government, union leaders and employer representatives said before a key jobs "summit" on Tuesday.

Dieter Hundt, president of the German Employers Federation, said that the government had in particular gone back on promises made last year to lower the high social security costs faced by employers when taking on staff.

"These promises have not been fulfilled in the last 14 months," Hundt told German radio, referring to the failed "Alliance for Jobs" pact early last year that sought to link job creation to moderate wage demands by German unions.
German wage costs are among the highest in the world -- a fact that the country's unions argue is offset by its high productivity levels.

The jobs alliance, which was sponsored by the government and followed talks between employers, unions and even church groups, fell apart early last year when the trade unions balked at state spending cuts later announced by Kohl.

The austerity package, designed to ease Germany's entry into the planned single European Union currency, included measures such as a proposed 20 percent to sick pay entitlements and other welfare entitlements, but Hundt said these had not eased the burden of non-wage costs on employers.

The two-day Berlin jobs summit, which will include speeches from senior politicians as well as employers and union leaders, starts as the German Federal Labour Office said earlier on Tuesday that unemployment slipped by 15,000 to a seasonally adjusted 4.3 million in March.

German central bank figures, also issued on Tuesday, put the seasonally adjusted jobless rate at 11.2 percent of the workforce, down from 11.3 percent in February. Unadjusted Labour Office data put the rate at 11.7 percent, down from 12.2 the previous month.
Despite the fall, the labour office said there was little sign that the economy was creating new jobs.

Leading trade union officials joined Hundt in criticism of the Kohl government, with Klaus Zwickel, head of the mighty IG Metall trade union, saying that Bonn's current policies would not bring about the hoped-for reduction in joblessness over the next few years.
Speaking on German radio, the metal and engineering union chief said the government's goal of cutting unemployment in half by the year 2000 was "in no way achievable" at the current rate.
Ursula Engelen-Kefer, deputy chief of the German Trade Union Federation (DGB), which is hosting the Berlin event, urged the government not to reduce public investment in infrastructure projects.

Existing cuts in public building spending had already led to "sickening unemployment in the construction sector, which also clearly brings with it joblessness in other sectors," she said on local Berlin radio.
Engelen-Kefer said a reduction in the millions of hours of overtime worked by Germans, as well as a shorter working week, would lead to a fairer sharing out of work among the population.
But employer groups reject such solutions, saying that long-term only if German industry is internationally competitive can jobs be protected.

The Berlin summit will include contributions from Wolfgang Schaueble, the powerful parliamentary leader of Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU), as well as Rudolf Scharping, his opposite number in the rival SPD party.
Representatives of some of Germany's largest companies are also scheduled to attend the event, as are leaders of the country's influential church groups.
